market_sizing.target_buyer: Owner-operator or operations manager of a small-to-mid sheet metal / job shop (10–80 employees). Decision typically made by founder/MD with strong input from estimator and shop foreman.
market_sizing.business_count_au: Roughly 2,000–3,000 small-to-mid metal fabrication shops in AU. IBISWorld and industry data put structural steel fabricators alone at 2,000+; the broader 'Fabricated Metal Product Manufacturing' ANZSIC subdivision (22) covers sheet metal job shops, plate work, and architectural metal products. Total AU metal fabrication market is ~AUD 665m (2024) growing at ~4.5% CAGR to ~AUD 1.03bn by 2034.
market_sizing.business_count_global: Conservatively 100,000+ small fabrication / job shops globally. US alone has ~25,000–30,000 NAICS 332710/332323 establishments; UK has ~6,000–8,000; Canada ~5,000. The FMA (Fabricators & Manufacturers Association) has ~2,300 corporate member companies in North America as one proxy.
market_sizing.typical_size: 5–80 employees, AUD 1m–20m annual revenue. Sweet spot is 15–50 staff and AUD 3m–12m revenue — too big for spreadsheets, too small for SYSPRO/Epicor.

pricing_reality.incumbent_pricing: Steelhead Technologies: starts ~USD 500/mo (entry tier), typical deployments USD 1.5k–5k/mo. Paperless Parts: custom pricing, real-world deals USD 600–2,000/mo for quoting alone. ProShop ERP: per-user pricing typically USD 150–250/user/mo, full deployments USD 2k–8k/mo. JobBOSS² (ECi): USD 200/user/mo + implementation. Fishbowl: perpetual license from USD 4,395 + USD 329/mo support, or subscription ~AUD 500/mo. Katana: from USD 99/mo (entry) but scales fast with users. Tier-1 ERPs (Epicor Kinetic, SYSPRO) start ~USD 4k/mo and require 6–12 month implementations.
pricing_reality.willingness_to_pay: AU shops will pay AUD 250–600/mo for a credible all-in-one quote/job/inventory tool, and AUD 800–2,000/mo as they hit 20+ staff. Pain is real: shops openly say ERP is 'clunky', 'JobBoss for 16 years and would not recommend', complain about USD 10k+ wasted on ProShop. A modern, well-priced AU product can land in the AUD 300–500/mo entry band and expand from there.
pricing_reality.sales_motion: Hybrid inside sales + content/SEO + trade show presence. Self-serve trial possible for entry tier, but >AUD 500/mo deals typically need 2–3 demo calls and a free pilot. Some shops are reachable cold (publicly listed phone/email, ABN lookup).
pricing_reality.realistic_arpu_au: AUD 350–500/mo blended ARPU at maturity. Entry plan ~AUD 249/mo, mid AUD 499/mo, multi-site AUD 999+/mo.
pricing_reality.expansion_revenue_potential: Strong. (1) Per-seat expansion as shop grows 10→40 staff. (2) Embedded payments on customer invoices (Stripe/Airwallex) — fab shops invoice AUD 1m–10m/yr, 1–2% take-rate is meaningful. (3) Materials marketplace / steel mill rebates. (4) AI quoting add-on (Paperless Parts-style geometry-based pricing) — easily a USD 200–400/mo upsell. (5) Capital / invoice finance partnerships. Plausible 2–3× ARPU expansion path.

competitive_landscape.incumbents: 1) **Steelhead Technologies** (US, founded 2020) — fastest-growing vertical-specific ERP for finishing/job shops; raised USD 6m Series A (2023), USD 12.5m Series B (2024), and USD 84m growth from Mainsail Partners (Dec 2025). Pricing from USD 500/mo. Limited AU presence today. 2) **Paperless Parts** (US, 2017) — quoting + estimation, strong AS9100 traceability story, mostly US shops, minimal AU footprint. 3) **ProShop ERP** (US/CA, ~2016 SaaS) — full ERP/MES/QMS, popular with regulated US shops, polarising UX ('time-consuming, abandoned after USD 10k'). 4) **JobBOSS² / E2** (ECi, US, 1987-era roots) — entrenched but widely complained about ('clunky', 'UI not intuitive'); very rebattable. 5) **Hypertherm ProNest** — nesting CAD/CAM with quote/work-order modules; integrates with most ERPs but not a full ERP. 6) AU-specific: **Jobman** (timber/cabinet leaning, has MYOB integration), **Workguru**, **Tradify** (too tradie-light). Generic mid-market: Fishbowl, Katana, Cin7. **No dominant AU-native sheet metal / job shop SaaS exists.**
competitive_landscape.incumbent_age_years: JobBOSS / E2 lineage ~38 years (founded 1987 as E2 Shop System). ProShop ~20+ years (started as internal tool, SaaS-ified mid-2010s). Steelhead 6 years. The dominant entrenched player (JobBOSS) is >15 years old — classic UI-rot opportunity.
competitive_landscape.user_satisfaction_signals: Practical Machinist and Reddit threads are filled with anti-incumbent sentiment: 'used E2 for 16 years, would not recommend to my worst enemy'; 'UI is not intuitive, search functions confusing'; 'inconsistent color coding for work item statuses'; 'all material treated as in-house inventory whereas we order based on BOM' (job shops don't fit production-ERP assumptions); 'ProShop was so insanely time consuming, USD 10k+ invested before abandonment'. ProShop and Steelhead get more positive reviews but Steelhead is finishing-shop heavy. Owners openly say they 'haven't found an ERP cost-effective and suited for their needs'.
competitive_landscape.recent_funding_or_ma: Major: Steelhead Technologies — USD 84m growth investment from Mainsail Partners (Dec 2025), following USD 12.5m Series B (2024) and USD 6m Series A (2023). Paperless Parts raised USD 50m Series C in 2022 (no fresh raise reported in 2025–26 window). Xometry (marketplace, adjacent) hit USD 687m FY2025 revenue (+30% YoY). ECi (JobBOSS owner) is PE-owned (Leonard Green). Active consolidation; the category is clearly being funded but predominantly US.
competitive_landscape.ai_disruption_risk: Moderate-to-high. Paperless Parts is pushing AI geometry-based pricing; Xometry uses ML for marketplace quoting; Steelhead is investing heavily post-USD 84m raise; multiple AI-native quoting startups (e.g. AutoQuote3D, Phasio for additive) are emerging. The window for a generic AI quoting tool is closing fast, but a localised AU/NZ ERP that bundles AI quoting + Xero/MYOB + nesting integration is still wide open.

opportunity_quality.core_pain: The unsolved workflow is **quote-to-cash for one-off and low-volume jobs**: estimator opens DXF/STEP in nesting software (SigmaNest/ProNest), guesses material+labour, drops a quote into Excel/email, then re-keys job into accounting (Xero/MYOB) once won, prints a paper traveller, scribbles statuses, and chases material from a separate spreadsheet. Travellers get lost, jobs get re-quoted at the wrong rate, traceability for ISO 9001 / AS9100 is reconstructed from memory. Shops use a combination of Excel, paper travellers, WhatsApp for shop-floor updates, and Xero — exactly the gap between Fishbowl/Katana (too product-centric) and Epicor/SYSPRO (too heavy).
opportunity_quality.moat_source: (1) Deep nesting/CAD integration (ProNest, SigmaNest, Lantek) — hard to fake, owners trust integrated solutions. (2) AU accounting depth (Xero + MYOB) — global tools have weak AU GST/payroll/STP2 fits. (3) Job-traveller data accumulates and becomes the operating system of the shop — switching cost. (4) AS9100 / ISO 9001 audit-trail records that span 7+ years — once these live in the system, ripping them out is painful. (5) Embedded payments + supplier connections (BlueScope, OneSteel, Stramit) become a network. No single source is huge; the bundle is.
opportunity_quality.critical_integrations: Must-have: Xero, MYOB, Stripe/Airwallex, ProNest or SigmaNest (DXF/quote import), email + PDF quote out, basic CAD viewer (STEP/IGES/DXF), Microsoft 365 / Google Drive. Nice-to-have: ABN Lookup, Bluescope/OneSteel material pricing feeds, AusPost/Sendle shipping, Square (POS for cash-and-carry sales).
opportunity_quality.incumbent_ehr_lock_in: Low. Most AU sheet metal shops are NOT locked into a vertical ERP — they're on Xero/MYOB + spreadsheets, or stuck on legacy MRP they actively want to leave. Rip-and-replace is realistic; no equivalent of EHR data lock-in.

build_difficulty.regulatory_complexity: Moderate. ISO 9001 traceability is normal for shops serving construction/mining/defence. AS9100 (aerospace, ~Clause 8.5.2) requires unique identifiers, full material lot-to-shipment traceability, 20–40 year records — meaningful but well-documented. Defence (DISP) and food-grade work add modest extras. WHS/welding standards (AS/NZS 1554, AS/NZS 3834) are workflow, not software, requirements.
build_difficulty.regulatory_changes_2025_2026: No single hard forcing function comparable to NDIS Support at Home. Worth tracking: (1) Mandatory climate-related financial disclosures under AASB S2 phased in from Jan 2025 (largest), Jul 2026 (mid), Jul 2027 (small) — many mid-fab shops will need Scope 1/2/3 emission reporting tied to materials and energy use; ERP that captures this is a wedge. (2) Modern Slavery Act reporting thresholds tightening (AUD 50m revenue → likely AUD 100m staying, AUD 50m+ supply-chain audit). (3) AS9100 Rev E draft expected late 2026. (4) NSW/Vic e-invoicing (Peppol) mandates rolling for B2B by 2027. None individually force ERP buying, but the climate-reporting one is real and recurring.
build_difficulty.domain_depth: Moderate. Outsider can become credible in 6–12 months by attending AMW (Australian Manufacturing Week), shadowing 5–10 shops, and learning the nesting/cutting workflow. Founder fit (Manuva background) is materially relevant — same general manufacturing-ops mental model. Less arcane than e.g. funeral or vet software.
build_difficulty.mvp_effort: 6–9 months solo / 4–6 months with 2 engineers for a credible v1: quote → job → traveller → invoice loop with Xero sync, DXF import, and basic shop-floor status. Production scheduling and AS9100-grade traceability are v2.
build_difficulty.technical_risks: Real but bounded: (1) Reliable DXF/STEP parsing and basic feature-detection for AI-assisted quoting — non-trivial; can leverage open-source libs (FreeCAD, OCCT) or buy via Paperless-style geometry APIs. (2) Two-way nesting integration (ProNest export/import) — well-documented file formats. (3) Real-time shop-floor input (tablets, scanners) — solved problem. No truly hard ML/routing problems unless you build full nesting yourself (don't).
build_difficulty.state_by_state_variance_au: Low for software logic. WHS regs differ by state but they're enforced at the shop level, not in software. Payroll/STP2 is federal. No need for multiple rule engines.
build_difficulty.data_residency_requirement: Not legally required for general manufacturing. Defence work (DISP) may require AU-hosted data — Supabase AU region (Sydney) covers this; a defence-tier add-on can be deferred.

distribution_difficulty.channel_options: (1) **Trade shows** — Australian Manufacturing Week (Brisbane May 2026, Sydney 2027) is the centrepiece, ~AUD 8k–15k for a small booth; AMTIL's AusTech and Weld Australia events. (2) **AMTIL's AMT magazine** — ~7,000 distribution, sponsored content / ads. (3) **Cold outbound** — ABN/ABR data is public, shop emails findable via websites + ABN Lookup, decent fit for 50-call/wk founder-led outbound. (4) **Content/SEO** — 'nesting software AU', 'sheet metal quote template', 'AS9100 traceability AU' all winnable. (5) **Channel** — partnerships with Hypertherm/ProNest resellers, BlueScope distributor reps, Xero advisor network. (6) **Reddit/Practical Machinist** — niche but engaged. (7) Industry Facebook groups exist but are small.
distribution_difficulty.trade_association_count_au: 5–8 active: AMTIL, Weld Australia, Australian Steel Institute (ASI), AMGA (Australian Made), Ai Group (broader), Manufacturing Australia, plus state-level e.g. SAMA (SA).
distribution_difficulty.trade_publication_count: ~5–10 with sponsorship slots: AMT magazine (AMTIL, ~7k circulation), Manufacturers' Monthly, @AuManufacturing newsletter, Australian Steel, The Fabricator (US but read in AU), Weld Australia Australian Welding journal.
distribution_difficulty.industry_facebook_group_size: Small. Groups like 'Sheet Metal Fabrication Australia', 'Australian Welders' etc. typically a few thousand members each; total reachable audience ~10k–25k. Not the primary channel.
distribution_difficulty.conference_event_count_au: 3–5 sub-$10k options: AusTech, Australian Manufacturing Week (booth varies), Weld Australia annual conference, AMTIL state expos, ASI National Convention. Plus a long tail of regional fab-shop opens.
distribution_difficulty.cold_outbound_viability: High. Shops are public-facing B2B businesses — websites, ABNs, phone numbers all listed. Decision-makers (owners) are findable on LinkedIn. Apollo/ZoomInfo cover ~40–60% of the segment. Cold email + targeted LinkedIn is workable.
distribution_difficulty.founder_market_fit_proxy: Good. Sheet-metal shop owners are open to outsiders who 'speak shop', understand DXF/nesting/cutting, and respect tradesperson culture. Demonstrating actual production-floor knowledge (visiting shops, knowing the tools) buys instant credibility. Less insider-gated than vet, funeral, or healthcare.
distribution_difficulty.case_study_acquisition_cost: Moderate. First 5 paying references probably require founder-led outreach to ~50–100 shops, 20–30 demos, and 3–6 month pilots — but free pilots are accepted in the segment. Likely 3–6 months of focused effort.
distribution_difficulty.content_seo_competitiveness: Moderate. AU long-tail ('nesting software Australia', 'sheet metal quoting Xero', 'AS9100 software AU') is winnable. Generic 'job shop software' is dominated by Steelhead/ProShop/Paperless Parts. Focused AU SEO is realistic.
distribution_difficulty.insurer_or_gatekeeper_dependency: None material. No gatekeeper API stands between you and the shop. Optional integrations (ProNest, Lantek, Xero) all have published APIs or are reverse-engineerable via file import.

personal_fit.manuva_data_model_reuse_pct: ~60–70%. Direct reuse: tenants, RLS, users/roles, suppliers, items, BOMs (treat as routings), locations/bins, production orders, activity_log. New: nesting-job records, traveller/QR scan events, customer-supplied material handling, certificates of conformity, AS9100 traceability lots. The core manufacturing-ops schema is highly relevant; production-order semantics shift from MTS (make-to-stock) to MTO (make-to-order).
personal_fit.manuva_code_reuse: High. Next.js 15 App Router, Supabase RLS, getServerTenantContext(), CSS Modules design system, server actions, activity_log pattern, invite flows, Xero/MYOB integration patterns all transfer cleanly.
personal_fit.buyer_persona_overlap_with_manuva: Partial. Manuva today targets discrete-product manufacturers with BOMs and inventory; sheet metal job shops are adjacent but distinct (MTO not MTS, customer-supplied material common, no long-run inventory). Could be cross-sold to Manuva customers who also do small batch fabrication, but mostly a fresh GTM with a separate marketing surface.
personal_fit.adjacency_to_manufacturing: Very close — same operations vocabulary (BOM, WIP, routings, suppliers), same accounting integrations, same shop-floor mental model.
personal_fit.technical_moat_durability_months: 9–18 months. AI-coding-tool-equipped competitor could replicate quote/job/invoice loop in 6–9 months, but nesting integrations, AU accounting depth, customer references, and accumulated traveller data buy real time. Moat compounds with each year of audit-trail data.

unit_economics.gross_margin_sensitivity: Healthy. Core SaaS workflow is mostly CRUD + integrations — 85%+ gross margin achievable. AI quoting (geometry analysis) is the only meaningful inference cost: ~AUD 0.10–0.50 per quote depending on model and complexity; chargeable as an add-on tier. No SMS/voice/human-in-loop dependencies in core product. Email and PDF rendering are cheap.
unit_economics.multi_location_natural: Moderate. Most shops are single-location; ~15–25% of mid-tier shops have 2–3 sites (e.g. Sydney + regional, or fab + finishing). Some grow via acquisition. Multi-site is an expansion lever but not the default.
unit_economics.churn_risk: Low-to-moderate. Job shops are sticky once data and travellers accumulate. Failure modes: shop closure (real — fabrication is cyclical, exposure to construction/mining), founder retirement (~25% of AU shops are owner-operators near retirement age), and switching to a competitor after a bad pilot. Expected gross churn 5–10%/yr.
unit_economics.customers_needed_for_target_arr: At AUD 400/mo blended ARPU: ~210 paying customers for AUD 1m ARR. At AUD 600/mo (with payments/AI add-ons): ~140 customers. Realistic given a 2,000–3,000 shop TAM in AU — 5–7% penetration.
